summary: Pupils aged 9-10 identify 3-D shapes (cubes and other cuboids, prisms, pyramids) from 2-D representations such as nets and isometric drawings. The core challenge is coordinating spatial visualisation (mentally folding/rotating) with explicit property knowledge (a cube has six square faces; opposite faces never share an edge). The persistent obstacle is 'look'-driven judgement — deciding 'it looks like a box' instead of reasoning from faces and checking a net actually closes. Teaching should start hands-on (cut and fold real nets, build with interlocking pieces) and then train a deliberate anticipation strategy: fix a base face, rotate the others up, and predict which faces meet and which end up opposite.
misconceptions: Judging the shape by the overall 'look' of the 2-D drawing rather than reasoning from faces/properties
Assuming any arrangement of six squares folds into a cube, without checking it closes without overlaps or gaps
Not anticipating which faces will meet or become opposite — no mental folding, just face-counting
Failing to recognise a solid drawn in a non-standard orientation (prototype/orientation bias)
Treating a flat net as a 2-D shape (its silhouette) rather than a foldable surface of a solid

activities.title: Fold real nets by hand: valid vs look-alike
steps: Cut out and fold a real cube net from paper or card and check it closes with no gaps or overlaps
Fold a look-alike net that has the same six squares but in which two faces overlap or leave a gap, and observe that it refuses to close
Before folding each net, choose a base face and say aloud which face you think will land opposite it, then fold to check
Build a cube-shaped solid and a triangular prism from interlocking construction pieces (e.g. polydron), joining flat faces until the solid closes
activities.insight: Having six squares is not enough — the arrangement must actually fold into a closed solid. Folding real nets makes the fold relationships concrete before pupils are asked to imagine them.

activities.title: Anticipate the fold: choose a base, rotate the rest up
steps: Choose a base face on a flat net and state the rule you are using (a cube has exactly six square faces; opposite faces do not share an edge)

Mentally fold each remaining face up along its hinge edge (faces joined to the base first, then the faces joined to those) and predict which faces will meet at each edge and which face lands opposite the base
Write or say your prediction for the finished solid before folding, then fold the real net to check

Optionally, on a controllable folding animation, drag a slider so the faces hinge upward around your chosen base and watch valid nets click shut while invalid ones collide or gap; use the ghost-preview that highlights which face lands opposite the base before folding, and spin the finished solid with a rotate handle
activities.insight: A reliable method replaces guessing: fix a base, rotate faces up, anticipate which meet and which become opposite, then confirm the net closes.

activities.title: Recognise solids in any orientation and link representations
steps: Name the 3-D shape shown in isometric drawings of the same solid in several different orientations, including non-standard ones (e.g. a cuboid drawn at an angle or resting on an unfamiliar face)
Justify each name by its faces/properties rather than by matching a single prototypical picture
Go both directions: predict the solid from a given net, and sketch or point to a valid net for a given solid
Optionally use a wrap/unwrap view — fold a net onto a rotatable solid and turn the solid to confirm it is the same shape whichever face it rests on, keeping a flat-net view alongside
activities.insight: A shape is defined by its faces and properties, so it stays the same shape in any orientation and across net, solid and isometric representations.

activities.title: Diagnostic check: which net folds into a cube?
steps: Given three flat shapes — one that folds into a closed cube, one missing a face, and one with six squares where two would overlap so it won't close — choose which folds into a cube and explain how you can tell

Answer probe questions: 'Point to the face that ends up opposite this one — how do you know?', 'This also has six squares — why doesn't it make a cube?', 'If I turn the cube onto a different face, is it still a cube? How can you tell?'
Check your answer by cutting and folding the net you chose
activities.insight: Reasoning from properties and mentally folding to check closure distinguishes a genuine understanding from an appearance-based guess.

checkQuestion: Put three flat shapes in front of the child: one folds into a closed cube, one is missing a face, and one has six squares but two would overlap so it won't close. Say: 'Which one folds into a cube? Explain how you can tell.'
checkAnswer: Picks the valid cube net and justifies it by mentally folding — fixing a base face, rotating the others up, and checking that six square faces close with no gaps or overlaps (and which faces end up opposite) — rather than by which arrangement 'looks most like a cube'. Correctly rejects the five-face net (a face is missing) and the overlapping six-square net (it won't close).
